messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: threading for nested AD calculations?
parts:
Hi!

I know that attempts to parallelize the autodiff stack usually cause big headaches, but has it been considered if it is possible to do nested autodiff calculations in different threads in parallel.

My hope with this would be to be able to perform nasty ODE integration (or any other expensive operation) in parallel over multiple threads.

So given AD calculations can be split into many independent and nested blocks, could one hope to have a chance to parallelize AD over threads then?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] threading for nested AD calculations?
parts:
Hi!

So this is a, let's say, realistic endeavour to make AD work in different threads given AD calculations are nested?

Wrt. to threading: If C++11 is available, then TinyThread is certainly an option. However, TinyThreads promotes itself to avoid a boost dependency. As we already have boost anyway, we could consider boost threads, right? To my understanding boost threads works accross all platforms, it just uses a different implementation on windows/non-windows.

The only caveat with it is that boost threads depends on some parts being build as a library, but this means that one would need to figure out a smart makefile for this which seems doable (given that we managed sundials/CVODE).

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] threading for nested AD calculations?
parts:
Possible, but a major undertaking. The key work will be
in synchronizing updates to the single autodiff tree from
the asynchronous parallel workers and figuring out how to
indicate in a model what can be done in parallel. So we'd
need someone who understands threading.

Given that in our standard use case (researcher on desktop
or notebook running 4 chains) we're out of parallel computing
power. So we've never prioritized multithreading.

C++11 won't be available until we can get it working for
all of our platforms and interfaces. As soon as the RStan
and PyStan developers give us the sign off and we can get
Windows building C++11, we can move over. I'd love to have
C++11 tools. And I'm afraid Eigen and Boost are going there
without us anyway.

- Bob

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] threading for nested AD calculations?
parts:
Hi Bob!

Well, computing power is ever to increase, so are laptops,to get more cpus soon... And in modern computer clusters you can easily parallelize over 20 or more cores on a single machine. Only with threading you will make Stan scale to large problems.

My initial thought was to go poor mans approach, so instead of figuring out autmatically what can be thrown into threads, I would instead somehow augment the language. Notmsure yet how, maybe a parallel_for or whatever turns out to be smart after some research, a prototype and some discussions.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] threading for nested AD calculations?
parts:
> On Mar 4, 2016, at 5:22 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob!
>
> Well, computing power is ever to increase, so are laptops,to get more cpus soon

It's not really happening on notebooks due to power
consumption issues --- just on servers, where we're
getting more cores.
> ... And in modern computer clusters you can easily parallelize over 20 or more cores on a single machine. Only with threading you will make Stan scale to large problems.

What's funny is that everyone tells us a different thing is
the key to scaling. There are really three candidates. The
first two fall under making our current horse (er, algorithm)
run faster:

THREADING
Use multiple threads in a single process to make one chain go faster
- could do this by parallelizing log-density/gradient calcs
- parallelizing operations like matrix multiply/solve
- running more exploration in parallel (faster adaptation, typical set
finding, etc.) and allowing shared adaptation

GPUs
Again, we'd have to do the same kind of threading as above.


Then there's developing approximate algorithms, which is Andrew's
current hobby horse (I hope you appreciate today's equestrian theme).

Then there's building a horseless carriage (er, new algorithm),
where we have two candidates:

STOCHASTIC DATA STREAMING
Run subblocks of the data sequentially a la Robbins-Monro (e.g.,
Matt's stochastic VB)

DATA PARALLEL SOLUTIONS
Run data in parallel (e.g. Andrew's EP-like algorithms)

> My initial thought was to go poor mans approach, so instead of figuring out autmatically what can be thrown into threads, I would instead somehow augment the language. Notmsure yet how, maybe a parallel_for or whatever turns out to be smart after some research, a prototype and some discussions.

That's a very rich poor person! But yes, it'd be great if we
could do any of the above things. Word on the street is that GPUs
is where the action's at. We've got gazillions (well tens of
thousands of them) on our cluster.

I'll reiterate that for the first two approaches, the trick is
going to be synchronizing the updates to the single autodiff stack.
Or figuring out how to also parallelize the reverse-mode step of
propagating derivatives.

- Bob

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] threading for nested AD calculations?
parts:
Hi Bob!

Thanks for this summary, very informative. And sorry for sounding like threading would be the only thing to make Stan scale. This is certainly something which gave me in my past always very good performance and I think, given that Stan is typically used for hierarchical models, a parallel_for can help a lot in many typical models written in Stan.

Moreover, we have a cluster with hundreds of CPUs such that getting Stan running on those in parallel would be a reall jump forward. Of course, GPU approaches may even be better... that's well possible.

BTW, using the compiler extension openMP could also be an alternative for a platform independent way of threading for loops... From my experience openMP is very easy to use and openMP 3.0 is supported by all the compilers we care about (as I can tell on a quick look). Let's see, maybe this is worth a try.

Sebastian
